ox: Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays bound to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. High glucose also keeps cAMP low. Transcription is off.
Wrong. Lactose releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is not activated. You get only low-level transcription. Trap: thinking lactose alone is enough.

Correct. Lactose becomes allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. Low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and helps RNA polymerase bind. Both signals together give maximum transcription.
Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays on the operator. Low glucose would make CAP active, but the gene is still blocked.

p: The lac operon holds genes to digest lactose. It has two controls. A repressor protein blocks the gene unless lactose (as allolactose) is present. That is negative control.

CAP is an activator. It works only when cAMP is high, which happens when glucose is low. That is positive control. Bacteria prefer glucose, so they switch on lactose genes fully only when lactose is present and glucose is gone.

q10.eli: A light turns on only if two switches are both on: 'there is food I can use' and 'my favorite food is gone'.
mem: Lactose present: repressor off the operator
Glucose low: cAMP high: CAP active
Max expression needs lactose present AND glucose absent
q10.trap: Stopping once the repressor is released. You also need CAP activation, which needs low glucose.

ox: Wrong. No known DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 5' end. The direction is 5' to 3'. Trap: confusing the direction of the template read with the direction of the new strand.
Correct. DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3'-OH of the growing strand. So the new strand grows 5' to 3'. It reads the template 3' to 5'.
Wrong. Both leading and lagging strands are built 5' to 3'. The lagging strand just has to be built in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.
Wrong. DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing. It needs a primer, made of RNA by primase, to provide a free 3'-OH.

p: DNA strands have two different ends, called 5' and 3'. DNA polymerase can only attach a new nucleotide to the 3' end of an existing strand. So the new strand always grows from 5' toward 3'.
It also cannot start on its own. It needs a short RNA primer that gives it a 3'-OH to build on.

q7.eli: Building a train where you can only add cars to the back. You can never add to the front, and you need a first car already in place.
mem: Polymerase needs a primer with a free 3'-OH
q7.trap: Mixing up the template direction (read 3' to 5') with the direction of new synthesis (5' to 3').

ox: Wrong. Helicase unwinds the double helix. That unwinding is what creates the positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Trap: helicase causes the problem; it does not fix it.
Correct. Topoisomerase cuts one or both DNA strands, lets the DNA swivel to release tension, and then reseals the cut. This relieves the supercoiling.
Wrong. Ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, such as between Okazaki fragments. It does not release twisting strain.
Wrong. Primase makes short RNA primers so that polymerase can start. It has no role in supercoiling.

p: When helicase unwinds a stretch of DNA, the DNA ahead gets overwound and tight. This is called positive supercoiling. If it builds up, replication stalls.
Topoisomerase solves this. It briefly cuts the DNA, lets it spin to relax, and reseals it. In bacteria, gyrase is a topoisomerase targeted by some antibiotics.

q8.eli: If you pull two twisted rope strands apart, the rope ahead of you gets twisted tighter. Someone has to snip, untwist, and tie it back.
mem: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling by cutting and rejoining
Primase makes RNA primers; ligase seals nicks
q8.trap: Picking helicase because it is at the fork. It creates the strain; topoisomerase removes it.

ox: Wrong. A silent mutation changes the codon but still codes for the same amino acid. UAG codes for no amino acid, so this is not silent.
Wrong. Missense means a different amino acid is inserted. Here no amino acid is inserted. UAG is a stop signal.
Correct. UAG is a stop codon. Changing UAC (Tyr) to UAG ends translation early, so the protein is truncated. That is a nonsense mutation.
Wrong. A frameshift comes from adding or removing bases (not in multiples of 3), shifting every codon after it. Here one base was swapped, so the frame is intact.

p: A codon is three RNA bases that code for one amino acid. A point mutation swaps one base. Silent: same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid. Nonsense: a stop codon appears.
The stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA. If one appears early, translation ends early and the protein is shorter, usually non-functional.

q9.eli: A sentence with a typo that makes a different word is missense. A typo that puts a period in the middle of the sentence is nonsense: the sentence stops early.
mem: Silent: same amino acid; missense: different; nonsense: stop
Frameshift needs an insertion or deletion not divisible by 3
q9.mn: Stop codons: 'U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away' for UAA, UAG, UGA.
q9.trap: Calling it missense because one amino acid is replaced. Here it is replaced by a stop signal, not another amino acid.
